source.title: EarthPT: a time series foundation model for Earth Observation
source.authors: Michael J. Smith; Luke Fleming; J. Geach

record.tranche_reason: The study uses the Chinchilla scaling rule as a rule of thumb to choose the training-token count for EarthPT-700M, but does not derive or test a scaling law or compute-optimal allocation.
record.gate_note: Appendix B reports training Huber-loss curves for four EarthPT sizes and says the larger models are still learning at the end of training. These are training-loss curves, not held-out cross-entropy measurements, and the study does not fit power laws or test extrapolation. The forecasting and embedding results do not measure the claim versions. The paper also says an EO-specific scaling law remains future work.
record.test_reason: EarthPT uses the Chinchilla rule (about 20 tokens per parameter) to pick 14B tokens for the 700M model. It fits no scaling law. Appendix B plots training Huber loss for four sizes, 10M to 700M, all trained on the same token budget. The only scaling-related statements are qualitative: 'similar training behaviour with traditional LLMs' and 'larger models are still learning'. No power-law form, extrapolation, allocation or downstream-scaling result is reported, so no version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The main conclusion is that EarthPT-700M forecasts pixel-level reflectance well: median NDVI L1 error of 0.05, against 0.08 for a phase-folded baseline, over five months. Its embeddings are semantically meaningful. On scaling, the authors use Chinchilla as a rule of thumb and plan an EO-specific law. They argue that, if scaling laws hold, abundant EO data (about 10^15 tokens) means there is no data limit to scaling.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains an autoregressive Earth-observation time-series model using Huber loss, rather than measuring held-out language-model cross-entropy. It uses the Chinchilla rule as a training-size heuristic and does not fit scaling laws.

fits_no_version.finding: Training Huber loss curves for EarthPT at 10M, 100M, 300M and 700M parameters on the same token budget. The authors say larger models are still learning at the end of training.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Larger EO time-series transformers reach lower training loss and keep improving at about 15B tokens (qualitative, no fit).

record.peer_reviewed: Tackling Climate Change with Machine Learning workshop at NeurIPS 2023
record.problems: For the scaling claim, the reported curves are training Huber loss rather than held-out cross-entropy, numerical curve values and uncertainty are not stated, and no power-law fit or compute-optimal allocation test is reported.

untested.parts: No held-out loss versus parameters, tokens or compute, and no power-law fit.
No prediction of larger-run loss from smaller-run fits.
The Chinchilla allocation is assumed, not tested; there is no fixed-compute sweep.
Depth and width change together with size; there is no comparison at fixed parameter count.
Earth-observation time-series pretraining is a new modality, but no power-law form is fitted or checked. The authors say an EO-specific law is future work.
Forecasting and embedding results come from the 700M model only and are not related to scale or loss.
No comparison of fitting choices or exponents.

record.verdict_notes: I agree with the reader's T4 / uses_without_test. A reader might take Appendix B ('scaling tests') as a V5 test, but it reports training loss only, with no values and no fit. All sizes share one token budget, so the smaller runs are not compute-optimal either.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining loss or power-law relationship in parameters, tokens, or compute is tested.
No power-law fit on smaller runs is used to predict larger-run loss.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or loss-minimising parameter/token split is tested.
The study does not compare architecture details at fixed parameter count for their effect on loss.
The Earth-observation training runs do not establish that a power-law form holds in this modality; no such fit is reported.
The study does not test whether downstream task performance improves predictably with scale or pretraining loss.
No comparison of fitting choices, exponents, compute-optimal splits, or curve bending is performed.
